newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels drape banners proclaiming defiance.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels drape banners proclaiming defiance.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima unfurled banners early on Saturday, sending a message of defiance that appeared to fly in the face of optimism created by negotiations.

Under the cover of darkness, three men scurried across the roof of the diplomatic residence early on Saturday and draped four banners over a side wall, according to cameramen watching the mansion with night-vision lenses from a nearby building.
"Surrender is not the way of the Tupac Amaru (Revolutionary Movement (MRTA)," read one banner in bold red letters.
Another said: "Peruvians - remember that (President Alberto) Fujimori does not govern for the poor. Fight for your rights."
A third banner referred to the rebels' main demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades and compared their relatives to those of the 72 men held under the gun for the 74th day.
"The families of our prisoners are also waiting for them in their homes," the message said. The fourth banner could not be read.

The MRTA underlined their fresh defiance by hoisting a red and white flag emblazoned with a mace, a rifle and the image of Tupac Amaru -- an 18th-century Andean Indian who led an unsuccessful, bloody uprising against Spanish colonial rule before he was executed by being drawn and quartered.
One of the men who lowered the banners covered his face with a red and white MRTA bandana, another, wearing overalls, was shirtless while the third was dressed in shirt and pants, witnesses said.
Holed up in the fortified compound and with most lines of communication to the outside cut off, the MRTA has several times used banners to wage its propaganda war against the government.
But with talks between the two sides apparently making some progress, the rebels had refrained for over a month from such tactics.
The new messages ran directly counter to this week's upbeat mood that followed a series of face-to-face talks aimed at hammering out a peaceful solution to the siege.

With both sides bound to secrecy, details of the talks have been scarce but the negotiations' guarantors appeared optimistic after the last meeting on Thurdsay saying they "noted and appreciated the desire of the participants to achieve a solution."
An eighth round of talks were scheduled to begin on Monday.

Latin America's best known human rights group had hoped to play a mediating role at those negotiations, but after a week of rebuffs the Buenos Aires-based Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo finally announced on Friday that it was going home.
Bitter at being snubbed by President Alberto Fujimori, who refused to even see the group, the Mothers' delegation warned that it would charge Peru with human rights abuses.

"(The Mothers) are going to present a formal complaint (to international organisations) against the Peruvian government for its prisons and political prisoners," Hebe de Bonafini, the group's leader, said.

The rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 in a bid to force the government to free their comrades, whom they claim are living in inhuman conditions. They also demand an end to Peru's secret military court system that tries people accused of terrorism without allowing cross-examination of witnesses.
Fujimori has repeatedly ruled out considering the release of MRTA prisoners but has indicated he might make other concessions.

He has said he will not use force to end the siege unless harm is done to the remaining captives, who include his brother, envoys of Japan and Bolivia, two government ministers and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
